newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu names army PM in bid to impose authority.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu names army PM in bid to impose authority.

text.p: Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko, under growing pressure to quit, named a senior general as emergency rule prime minister on Wednesday in a move that had all the hallmarks of a last bid to cling to power.

With rebels in Zaire's economically-vital second city of Lubumbashi and Washington suggesting it was time for the veteran leader to go, Mobutu shunted aside his arch foe Etienne Tshisekedi after less than a week in the job.

His army blocked access to the prime minister's office complex in the capital, fired in the air and used tear gas to prevent thousands of Tshisekedi supporters taking the veteran opposition leader there to install his new government team.
"The new state of emergency is for the dustbin. Mobutu made the decision all alone," Tshisekedi's minister of posts and telecommunications, Modeste Kikunga, told Reuters.
"We won't take this lying down. They will find us in their path," one Tshisekedi aide said on hearing Mobutu had appointed General Likulia Bolongo prime minister in place of Tshisekedi.
A decree, signed by Mobutu one day after he declared a nationwide state of emergency, said Tshisekedi had lost the confidence of Zaire's political family.

Mobutu seized power in the sprawling Central African nation in 1965 but Laurent Kabila's rebels have steadily loosened his grip with a succession of victories -- the latest in Lubumbashi, capital of mineral-rich Shaba province.
The rebels, who took up arms in October vowing to topple him, now control almost half the country.
Mobutu's critics say that Zaire, potentially one of the richest countries in Africa, has been impoverished by corruption and mismanagement under his rule.

Ordinary Zaireans, hungry for change, hail Kabila as a liberator both inside and outside rebel-held areas but Tshisekedi, who spearheaded protests that forced Mobutu to embrace democratic change, still enjoys considerable support in Kinshasa and his diamond-rich home region of Kasai.

Likulia, a university professor and top army judge, was defence minister in the pre-Tshisekedi administration of Kengo wa Dondo. The transitional parliament voted out Kengo following persistent charges that he mismanaged the war in the east.
Tshisekedi fell foul of Mobutu supporters and allies alike after announcing a government composed of his own loyalists. He earmarked six posts for rebels but the offer was rebuffed.
On Wednesday, his eyes streaming from teargas, Tshisekedi tried to walk to the prime minister's office complex, which security forces blocked off with troops and armoured vehicles.
Security forces fired in the air and used teargas after the crowd burst through an initial security cordon.

Witnesses said that Mobutu's son Kongolo, a presidential guard officer known in Kinshasa as "Saddam Hussein" after the Iraqi leader, had escorted Tshisekedi back home. Tshisekedi was bleeding from a wound to the head, one aide said.
In Goma, rebel spokesmen said the fall of Lubumbashi spelt the collapse of Mobutu's rule.
The United States signalled it was time for Mobutu to step down, effectively ending a decades-old alliance with the African strongman dating back to the Cold War and fears of the spread of Communism.
"Mobutuism is about to become a creature of history," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
